analysis.one_liner: Bans the manufacture, sale, and use of commercial asbestos nationwide, with a short transition for the chlor-alkali industry.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee after being introduced in March 2023; no vote was ever taken.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Toxic Substances Control Act to ban making, processing, using, or selling commercial asbestos and any products containing it, effective one year after enactment. Facilities that use asbestos in chlorine production would get two more years to import and use it. The President could grant limited national-security exemptions, and the EPA would have to publish public education materials about asbestos health risks. The bill was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee on the day it was introduced and never advanced further.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people are the main beneficiaries. Asbestos exposure causes mesothelioma and other cancers, and exposure often comes from workplaces, older buildings, and consumer products where individuals have little control over the materials used. By banning new manufacture and commerce in the six-plus commercial asbestos fibers, the bill would cut off new sources of exposure while leaving already-installed materials in place for compliant removal. Workers in demolition, renovation, and older industrial plants would face less exposure to newly introduced asbestos materials. People who already have asbestos in their buildings would get EPA-developed public education resources about health risks and how to find licensed abatement services.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers and residents exposed to asbestos

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits the manufacture, processing, use, and distribution in commerce of commercial asbestos and products containing it, effective one year after enactment [S2][S3].
Covers eight asbestos fiber types including chrysotile, the type still imported and used in the United States, rather than leaving any commercial form legal [S3].
Gives the chlor-alkali (chlorine production) industry two additional years to import and use asbestos for diaphragms, providing a transition while still ending that use [S3].

Requires the EPA, with HHS, to produce public education resources on asbestos health effects, federal prevention and mitigation resources, and where to find licensed asbestos abatement in each state [S2][S3].
Excludes asbestos already installed in buildings before enactment and disposal-only handling, so the ban targets new commerce rather than forcing removal of existing materials [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The chlor-alkali industry, which imports processed asbestos to make diaphragms for chlorine production, would have to convert to asbestos-free membrane technology within two years or stop those operations, bearing conversion costs that could affect chlorine and related product prices. Companies that manufacture or distribute products containing commercial asbestos would lose access to that material. Costs would be passed partly to consumers as higher prices or product reformulation.
analysis.who_pays_short: Chlor-alkali plants and asbestos product makers

drawbacks.text: The chlor-alkali industry uses asbestos diaphragms in chlorine production, and although the bill allows two years to transition, abrupt supply or cost effects on chlorine (used in water treatment and many products) were the main practical objection; the carve-out itself also keeps a known carcinogen in use through that window [S3].

The ban leaves asbestos already installed in buildings untouched, so people living or working in older structures with existing asbestos would still face exposure risks and would rely on voluntary abatement rather than any mandated removal [S3].

The President could grant national-security exemptions lasting up to three years, extendable once, with confidentiality carve-outs from publication, meaning the prohibition would not be absolute in all cases [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health benefit of stopping new commerce in a known carcinogen is large and long-lasting, since asbestos-related cancers develop decades after exposure and there is no established safe level. The costs are real but transitional: one industry (chlor-alkali) already had substitute technology available and would have gotten two years to convert, and installed asbestos would remain subject to existing removal rules. The main design weakness is that the bill does nothing about the enormous stock of asbestos already in buildings, but that is a limitation rather than a reason the ban itself fails to help the public.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee on the day it was introduced and no further action was ever taken on it.

narrative.text: Senator Merkley introduced the bill on March 30, 2023 [S1][S5].
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works that same day [S5].
No committee action, report, floor vote, or further consideration ever occurred, and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5].
Three Senate Democrats cosponsored the bill [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the chlor-alkali industry and any companies still selling asbestos-containing products avoided a mandated switch to alternatives, and their asbestos imports and sales could continue under existing rules. For the public, the known harm from continued asbestos commerce continued unaddressed by this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Asbestos users in industry and commerce

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; never took the bill up
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on March 30, 2023 and never acted on it, so it never reached the Senate floor.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never got a vote, so no one was recorded on the record as opposing it; its four listed supporters were all Democrats, and no Republican cosponsor ever joined [S4].

industries.note: These plants import chrysotile asbestos to make diaphragms used in chlorine production and are the main remaining U.S. users. The bill would give them two years to import and use asbestos before a full ban, forcing conversion to asbestos-free alternatives at their expense.

industries.industry: Manufacturers and distributors of asbestos-containing products
industries.note: A one-year deadline would end their ability to make, process, use, or sell commercial asbestos and products containing it, eliminating a low-cost raw material and the products built from it.

The bill requires EPA education resources about licensed commercial asbestos mitigation availability, directing the public toward licensed abatement services; removal of asbestos already in buildings continues regardless, so the abatement industry's core business is untouched.
